title: The DNA Feature-Proxy Disagreement Grid
takeaway: A random-sample grid crossing the DNA feature's activation level against whether the hand-built DNA proxy fires, used to audit the cases where the two disagree. The authors read all 24 disagreements and attribute 22 of them to the proxy's strict ATCG vocabulary rather than to the feature, leaving one genuine miss and one genuine false alarm. It is a hand-judged count of 48 examples, so it supports the claim that the feature is sensitive and specific for DNA rather than measuring it.
walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Eight boxes of text sit in two rows and four columns, above a thin colored strip.

The strip is the activation histogram for the [[dna-feature]] A/1/2937, which fires on long uppercase runs of A, T, C and G. Its horizontal axis is activation level, from the feature being off at 0 out to about 11.5. Each vertical slice is split by color: red is the share of tokens at that level where the [[dna-proxy]] fires, blue the share where it does not.

That proxy is a hand-built score, not a second model. It models DNA as a random string over ATCG, each base with probability $1/4$, and asks how much more likely a string is under that story than under ordinary text: $\log(P(s|\text{DNA})/P(s))$. The continuous score is then [[proxy-binarization]] — reduced to yes or no by its sign.

Red grows with activation across the strip. That growth is the [[activation-specificity]] claim. The blue at low activations is what the grid above exists to examine.

The four columns are four sampled activation levels, each joined to its place on the axis by a dotted line: off (0), then roughly 4.8, 7.1 and 11.4. The two rows are the proxy's verdict — pink on top for proxy active, blue below for proxy not active.

Each of the eight cells holds six dataset examples drawn at random from that combination, not the strongest ones, which is the point of the design: unlike a list of [[top-dataset-examples]], a random draw can show failures. Within an example, the bold token is the one being scored, four tokens of context sit on either side, and orange shading gives the feature's activation on each token.

### How to read it

Agreement lives in the bottom-left cell, where feature and proxy are both off, and in the top row of the three active columns, where both are on.

Disagreement lives in the other four cells. The top-left cell holds six cases where the proxy fires and the feature is off. The bottom row of the three active columns holds eighteen cases where the feature fires and the proxy does not.

### What it shows

The authors walk those 24 cases and blame the proxy in 22 of them. Spaces (" AAG"), dashes ("5'-"), square brackets and missing bases all break the strict ATCG model, though the text is plainly DNA. The feature also fires on "5'-", where DNA is about to start.

Two errors are marked as real. A red star flags one [[activation-sensitivity]] miss: genuine DNA the feature stays off for, though it starts firing on the next token. A blue star flags one false positive, "sgRNA target", which is DNA talk but not a nucleotide string.

terms.definition: The feature under study: feature number 2937 from dictionary learning run 1 on transformer A. The paper says it is the only feature in that run devoted to modeling DNA context.

The independently computed score for "is this a DNA sequence", equal to the log-likelihood ratio of the string under a DNA model versus under ordinary text. It is the yardstick the feature is checked against, and it is written by hand rather than learned.
The row of cells holding examples where the binarized DNA proxy came out positive. Its cells are shaded pink.
The row of cells holding examples where the binarized DNA proxy came out non-positive. Its cells are shaded blue.
The scalar value the sparse autoencoder's hidden unit takes on a token, after the ReLU. Here it both labels the histogram axis and selects which column of examples you are reading.
The leftmost column and the isolated bar at 0: tokens where the feature's activation is exactly zero. It is shown as its own bucket rather than folded into the low end of the continuum.
Within each slice of the bottom strip, the portion of tokens at that activation level for which the proxy fired. Red climbing toward the right is the specificity story in one picture.
The complementary portion of each slice: tokens at that activation level where the proxy did not fire. Blue at low activations is what the example grid is auditing.

The small filled dot and open circle just under the axis, separating the exactly-zero bucket from the continuum of positive activations. They mark that the leftmost bar is not part of the smooth distribution.
The four dashed lines running from each column of cells down to a point on the activation axis. They say which activation level the six examples in that column were sampled from.
Per-token shading inside an example, darker where the feature activates more strongly. It lets you see the feature switching on partway through a string.
Within each example, the single token whose activation put that example in this column. The surrounding tokens are context, four on each side.
The mark on the one case the authors count as a genuine failure of sensitivity: real DNA ("for: ATCGTGCGTGACATT") that the proxy flags and the feature misses.
The mark on the one case the authors count as a genuine failure of specificity: "sgRNA target BBL_gRNA_", where the feature fires on text about DNA that is not itself a nucleotide string.
Here, a token that really is part of a DNA sequence but on which the feature stays off. One such case is marked in the grid.
Here, a token on which the feature fires that the authors judge is not DNA. One such case is marked in the grid.
Snippets pulled at random from the tokens meeting a cell's condition, rather than the ones with the highest activation. Random sampling is what makes the grid capable of exposing errors.

terms.term: GCAT strings that are contextually not DNA
terms.definition: The column-1 caption's name for text such as "PISCATAWAY" or "GRETTA LEVINS", where letters from the ATCG alphabet happen to line up and the proxy fires even though no DNA is present. These are proxy errors, not feature errors.

The formatting the captions blame for the proxy going silent on real DNA — " AAG", "AC-3'", "5'-AAG", "AG[AG...]". Any character outside ATCG collapses the proxy's likelihood, while the feature keeps firing.

Standard biochemistry notation for the two ends of a nucleotide strand, appearing in examples like "5'-TCT". The feature fires on the prefix itself, which the authors read as it predicting the DNA that follows.

Guide RNA, terminology from gene editing that appears in the blue-starred example. It is molecular-biology vocabulary rather than a nucleotide sequence, which is why the authors count the feature's activation there as a real false positive.
The end-of-text token visible in one of the both-off examples. It appears only as ordinary tokenizer output in a random snippet.

The proxy reduced to a yes/no by taking the sign of its log-likelihood ratio, justified because the ratio's distribution turned out strongly bimodal. Every red/blue split in this figure is a split on that binary value.
The figure's term for a disagreement where the authors judge the feature to be at fault, as opposed to the many where they judge the proxy at fault.

numbers.meaning: The grid's shape: proxy active versus proxy not active, crossed with four sampled activation levels. Every cell is one combination of feature state and proxy verdict.
Random dataset examples shown in each cell. Six is enough to read quickly and small enough to fit eight times on a page; it is not a sample size chosen for statistical power.
Total examples on display, being 8 cells times 6 examples. This is the full evidence base for the figure's conclusion.
The activation level of the leftmost column, drawn as its own isolated bar: the feature is entirely off. It also serves as the threshold for the binarized proxy, whose sign decides red versus blue.

The three positive activation levels the other columns were sampled at, read off where their dotted lines meet the axis. They span the low-middle, middle and top of the feature's range so that purity can be compared across registers.
The range of the activation axis, i.e. the largest value this feature takes on the sampled data. The red share of the strip approaches all of it at the far right.
Examples in the top-left cell: cases where the proxy fires but the feature is off. All six sit in the feature-off column, so this cell is the entire sensitivity audit shown here.

Examples in the bottom row across the three active columns (3 x 6): cases where the feature fires but the proxy does not. The summary text on the right calls these "flagged by the proxy", which reads as loose wording, since the proxy is precisely what did not fire on them.
Disagreements the authors count as real errors of the feature, out of the 24 disagreements shown. The remaining 22 they attribute to the proxy's strict ATCG vocabulary.
The false negative rate implied by the top-left cell: one of the six proxy-positive, feature-off examples is genuine DNA the feature missed. The other five are strings the proxy misread.
The false positive rate implied by the bottom row: one of the eighteen feature-on, proxy-off examples is judged not to be DNA. The other seventeen are DNA the proxy's character model could not score.
The Pearson correlation between the binarized DNA proxy and the feature's activations, reported in the surrounding text. It is the single-number summary the grid is meant to explain the gaps in.
From the text just above: all ten random dataset examples with activation above 6.0 were DNA. This is why the figure spends its attention on the lower registers instead.

The probability the proxy assigns each of A, T, C and G under its DNA model, treating a sequence as uniform random bases. Any other character therefore drives the likelihood ratio sharply negative, which is the mechanism behind the spaces-and-dashes failures.

The minimum number of tokens the proxy is evaluated over, because single tokens such as CAT occur in ordinary English as well as in DNA. Grouping tokens is what keeps the proxy from firing on every stray codon-like word.
Tokens of context displayed on each side of the scored token in every example, per the paper's visualization appendix. It is why each snippet is a nine-token window rather than a full sentence.
The visualization dataset: a 100 million token subset of training data, taking only 10 tokens from each context. The random examples in the grid are drawn from this pool.
The number of learned features in run A/1 and the number of MLP neurons in transformer A. The feature shown, A/1/2937, is one of those 4,096 directions living in a 512-dimensional activation space.
